analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks and credit unions with up to $50 billion in assets from direct CFPB examinations.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee 39-21 and was placed on the House calendar in November 2017, but never received a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau directly examines and collects reports from any bank or credit union holding $10 billion or more in assets. This bill would raise that cutoff to $50 billion, freeing dozens of midsize banks and credit unions from direct CFPB supervision. Those institutions would still be examined for consumer-law compliance by their other federal regulators, but the bureau would no longer run the checks itself.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions with assets between $10 billion and $50 billion gain by escaping the CFPB's direct examinations and reporting requirements, reducing their compliance workload and regulatory exposure. Industry groups sought this as regulatory relief.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold for direct CFPB examination and reporting from $10 billion to $50 billion, so institutions between those sizes are no longer examined directly by the bureau.
Reduces compliance and reporting costs for dozens of midsize insured banks and credit unions that the 2010 law had placed under direct bureau supervision.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who bank with midsize institutions would bear the cost of thinner federal scrutiny: the CFPB, the dedicated consumer-law enforcer, would no longer directly examine banks between $10 billion and $50 billion for compliance with consumer financial protection laws, relying instead on prudential regulators who handle consumer-law checks among many other duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Customers of midsize banks and credit unions

drawbacks.text: Removing direct CFPB examinations for banks between $10 billion and $50 billion weakens dedicated oversight of how those institutions treat customers on mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer products.

The bill's defenders argue the $10 billion threshold imposed duplicative compliance costs on regional banks and credit unions, and that prudential regulators would still examine them for consumer-law compliance, so consumer protections would not disappear entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, direct benefit to a defined set of midsize financial institutions while spreading a subtler cost across their customers: less dedicated federal scrutiny of consumer-law compliance. Because other regulators would still examine these institutions, the loss of protection is real but partial, while the industry's gain in reduced compliance burden is immediate.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it on a 39-21 vote and it sat on the House calendar, but the full House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in June 2017 by Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay, a Democrat, with Rep. Steve Stivers, a Republican, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee held markups in October 2017 and ordered the bill reported on a 39-21 vote.
The committee reported the bill without amendment on November 21, 2017, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, meaning it was eligible for House floor consideration.
The House never took up the bill, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead in the narrow sense that direct CFPB examination of banks holding $10 billion to $50 billion in assets was never scaled back. The midsize banks and credit unions seeking relief from direct bureau supervision did not get it from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, who kept direct CFPB oversight

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor from a banking-region district paired with a Republican cosponsor, and the committee's 39-21 report vote, indicate the bill drew votes from both parties in committee, though the record does not list how each member voted.

industries.industry: Midsize banks and credit unions ($10 billion to $50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would free these institutions from direct CFPB examinations and reporting, cutting their compliance costs. Their gain comes from reduced federal scrutiny of their consumer-law compliance, so their interest runs against stronger oversight of how they treat customers.

The bureau would lose direct examination and reporting authority over dozens of institutions, narrowing the dedicated consumer-protection watchdog's reach. Its supervisory interest runs alongside stronger protection for bank customers.
